content: Microbial cultures, traditionally used for diagnosing neonatal sepsis, are limited by their low sensitivity and the time required to obtain results. Recent advancements in molecular microbiology have led to the development of molecular assays that are faster and may improve clinical outcomes for neonates. The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of various molecular methods for detecting culture-positive bacterial and fungal sepsis in neonates. Additionally, the study aimed to investigate differences among studies by analyzing subgroups based on gestational age, type of sepsis onset, and to compare the performance of different molecular tests. A systematic review was conducted following the guidelines of the Cochrane Diagnostic Test Accuracy Working Group. On January 19, 2016, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple electronic bibliographic databases, including the Cochrane Library, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL. Conference proceedings from the Pediatric Academic Societies annual conference, clinical trial registries (such as ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, and WHO ICTRP), and the Science Citation Index were also reviewed. Experts in the field were contacted to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria for the review were studies with prospective or retrospective cohort or cross-sectional designs that evaluated molecular assays in neonates with suspected sepsis. These molecular assays (index tests) were compared against microbial cultures, which served as the reference standard. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the included studies and extracted relevant data. Meta-analyses were performed using bivariate and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) models, and the data were analyzed using Review Manager 5 software. A total of 35 studies met the inclusion criteria. The pooled sensitivity of molecular assays was estimated to be 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.82 to 0.95), while the pooled specificity was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.89 to 0.96). These results were based on evidence of moderate quality. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity based on factors such as the type of molecular test, gestational age, type of sepsis onset, and sepsis prevalence. However, these analyses did not provide sufficient explanations for the observed heterogeneity, with evidence quality ranging from moderate to very low. Sensitivity analyses, which included studies using blood samples and those with robust methodologies, yielded similar results, further supporting the findings (moderate quality evidence). In conclusion, molecular assays offer the advantage of rapid diagnostic results and demonstrate good performance as supplementary tests for diagnosing neonatal sepsis.
